item.title: Amy Acton's estranged mom stars in a GOP attack ad. Their painful history spans decades.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A new campaign ad in which the estranged mother of Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton argues that her daughter should not be elected as the Buckeye State's next governor has added a new level of controversy to what was already one of the most closely watched races of the midterms. Acton, a Democrat, is running to replace outgoing Republican Gov. Mike DeWine. She's facing Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, a billionaire who ran an unsuccessful presidential campaign in 2024. In the ad, Acton's mother, Donna Arthur , calls her daughter a "liar" and urges Ohioans not to support her. "Don't let her become your governor," she says. "If you think she'll make your life better, you're fooling yourself. It will only get worse." As the ad began to spread across social media, Acton's brother released a statement in which he accused Arthur of siding with their stepfather after he was charged with sexually abusing Acton when she was a child, and criticized Ramaswamy for attempting to use that abuse as a "political talking point." Ramaswamy defended the ad on Tuesday, telling reporters that Acton's account of her past "does deserve to be scrutinized." His campaign confirmed to the Enquirer that it will spend $4 million to air the ad across the state. The ongoing controversy over the ad, which has been widely condemned by Democrats and sparked pushback from some Republicans, has put a new spotlight on the race for Ohio's top elected office. Ohio Sen. Jon Husted, an incumbent Republican locked in a tight reelection race, released a statement saying he personally “would not have run” the ad. Meanwhile, Vice President JD Vance, himself a former senator from Ohio, said Republicans who disapprove of the ad should “ stop whining ” and remember that politics is a “tough business” during a campaign stop in Cincinnati on Wednesday. Yahoo Once a key swing state, Ohio has steadily become redder in recent decades. Four years ago, DeWine won reelection by more than 25 percentage points . But polls suggest that Acton has a chance to break the GOP's long run of control over the Ohio Statehouse. Here's what you need to know about who she is, how her past informs what she stands for today and what the polls say about her chances of winning. Who is Amy Acton? Acton has been open about the "difficult" childhood she endured growing up in Youngstown, Ohio, in the 1970s. On her campaign website, she says she overcame "periods of abuse, hunger, and neglect, and even wound up living in a tent in the middle of winter." In 2019, she publicly discussed for the first time that she had been sexually assaulted by her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, between the ages of 9 and 12. After Acton's biological father reported the abuse in 1978, Arthur was arrested and charged with rape, according to contemporary news reports and court documents obtained by the Associated Press . Acton's mother sided with her stepfather, disputing the allegations of abuse. The couple left the state before Arthur could face trial and allegedly remained together until his death in 2004 . Both Acton and her mother say they have not seen or spoken to each other since a court hearing in which Acton testified against her stepfather nearly 50 years ago. "In the courthouse after they were charged, I went to give her a kiss, and she just turned her cheek away. That was the last time I ever saw her," Acton told the now-shuttered newspaper the Vindicator in 2019. Acton found more stability after moving in with her father and became a standout student in high school. She earned a bachelor's degree from Youngstown State University and a medical degree from the Northeast Ohio School of Medicine, working various jobs to pay her way through college. She completed residencies in pediatrics and preventive medicine before becoming a professor at Ohio State University , where she taught classes on maternal and child health. She also directed a community organization called Project L.O.V.E. to promote preventive health care among Columbus-area children. In 2019, DeWine tapped her to become director of the Ohio Department of Health. When the COVID-19 pandemic hit a year later, she advised DeWine to take swift action to control the spread of the virus. Under her guidance, Ohio became the first state in the nation to shut down all public schools. Acton also gained national attention thanks to the daily public briefings she gave throughout the early stages of the pandemic. In May 2020, an opinion piece in the New York Times called her "The Leader We Wish We All Had." Acton resigned a month later amid pressure from the Republican-led state legislature to sign orders rolling back COVID restrictions, moves she would later say "there was no science for." She briefly remained part of DeWine's administration as a public health adviser before leaving to resume working in the nonprofit sector. She announced her plans to run for governor in early 2025 and cruised through the Democratic primary in May. Acton was married to her first husband, with whom she had three children, for nearly 20 years before they divorced in 2008. She married her current husband in 2010 and became stepmother to his three children. What does Acton stand for? As a Democrat running in a conservative-leaning state, Acton fits firmly into the moderate wing of her party. Her policy platform focuses heavily on affordability, including proposals to lower the cost of health care, combat fraud, cut high energy bills and crack down on corporations that take advantage of workers and consumers. In July, she drew criticism from some progressive Democrats for saying that she supported barring transgender children from participating in girls' and women's sports. Soon afterward, she added language to her website pledging to protect Ohio's LGBTQ community, without directly contradicting her previously stated stance on transgender athletes' participation in sports. Acton has also spoken in favor of Ohio's voter ID requirements, a position that puts her at odds with many Democrats who view such laws as a voter suppression tactic by Republicans. Acton has also called for an increase in funding for police departments, more money for public schools and heavy investment in Ohio's rural and farming communities. What are her chances? Polling in the Ohio governor's race has fluctuated significantly as Election Day has grown closer. In the aggregate, the polls suggest that Acton has steadily widened her lead over Ramaswamy over the past several weeks. At the same time, two polls released in October show Ramaswamy ahead. The Cook Political Report and the Center for Politics , two of the country's top nonpartisan forecasters, list the race as a toss-up. No polls of the race have been conducted since the ad featuring Acton's mother became public, so it's too early to gauge what impact — if any — the controversy might have on voters' views of the two candidates. item.title: Peter Thiel breaks with Trump over Iran war: 'We should not have done it'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Billionaire technology investor Peter Thiel said he’s skeptical of the U.S. war with Iran and does not believe the United States should have launched it, putting the major Republican donor at odds with President Donald Trump over one of the administration’s defining foreign policy decisions. Thiel's remarks, delivered on Oct. 12 at a private event, are his most explicit statements to be revealed publicly about the war with Iran and come less than two weeks before the midterm elections in which Trump's party is grasping to maintain power in Congress. The audio of Thiel's comments was obtained by Decoded by POLITICO from a lecture earlier this month. “I’m skeptical of [the war], I think we should not have done it," Thiel said. "There were a lot of mistakes that were made.” Thiel added, “Maybe we don’t have the hard power. Maybe we’re going to lose the soft power war.” In the full lecture, Thiel made clear his strong opposition to neoconservatives and Middle East wars. Despite his criticism of the Iran war, Thiel highlighted his continued support of Trump and suggested he wanted to protect the president. Still, Thiel's break over the war represents one of the most important examples to date of a fierce Trump ally sharing deep concerns about the conflict. The comments were part of Thiel's lecture series in Nashville, which Decoded has documented since their start this fall . In the latest lecture, Thiel issued extensive warnings about what he described as the unchecked power of the International Criminal Court, drawing on comments from Bush-era figures Donald Rumsfeld and Dick Cheney. "I read the Cheney family's Trump derangement syndrome as an attempt to buy favor with the [International Criminal Court] and avoid prosecution. Probably too late,” Thiel said. “And I have come to suspect that the threat of an ICC arrest warrant is the sword of Damocles hanging over the Trump administration as it tries to persecute this war in Iran." Thiel also discusses meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in early 2024, after the Oct. 7 attack, where he said he asked the leader about his plans in Gaza. Thiel said Netanyahu told him, “I can’t just Dresdenize it,” referring to the Allied bombing of the German city of Dresden during World War II that killed roughly 25,000 people. The first big tech investor to back Trump in 2016, and then have a high-profile speaking role at the Republican National Convention that year, Thiel was also the biggest financial backer of super PACs supporting Vice President JD Vance’s Senate campaign in 2022. POLITICO reported in March that Vance was “skeptical” of the U.S. striking Iran in the lead-up to the beginning of the war. Representatives for Thiel and the White House did not respond to requests for comment. Read more from Thiel’s latest lectures in Thursday’s edition of Decoded by POLITICO , including his sentiments toward Israel and predictions for the 2028 election. item.title: Washington orders U.S. embassy staff to leave Saudi Arabia after near-daily Houthi attacks
item.description:

Saudi Arabia has faced near-daily attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis, including a strike on Riyadh's international airport that was the kingdom's deadliest in years (Giuseppe CACACE) The United States has ordered non-essential US embassy staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, the State Department said on Wednesday, as the kingdom comes under sustained deadly attacks by Yemen's Houthis. "Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said in a social media post explaining the measure. "The safety and security of Department personnel and their families remain our highest priority," he added. A diplomatic source in the Middle East told AFP that some families of US embassy personnel were also being withdrawn in the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain, but Pigott stressed that Wednesday's order was for the departure of non-emergency embassy staff and their families in Saudi Arabia only. Saudi Arabia has this month come under near-daily attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis, including a strike on Riyadh's international airport that was the kingdom's deadliest in years, as the war with the group escalates. On Wednesday, the Saudi energy ministry said that falling debris from the successful interception of a drone targeting an oil facility killed two people and injured a further two. "The attempted attack resulted in the deaths of two individuals, a Filipino and a Nepali, and injuries to two others," the ministry said in a statement. It did not say who launched the drone aimed at Shaybah oil field near the UAE border. Earlier on Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen reported intercepting six drones. One person was killed and eight others wounded in an attack on Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, aviation officials said. In June, a four-year-old truce in Yemen's civil war collapsed, reviving the conflict that dates back to 2014. The Saudi-led coalition has backed the internationally recognized government since 2015. - Iran explosions - The US previously ordered non-essential staff to leave the Gulf ahead of the start of its war against Iran in late February and again in July before US President Donald Trump called off a new wave of strikes. Late on Wednesday, Iranian state media reported the sound of explosions in the southern Hormozgan province overlooking the Strait of Hormuz, breaking a spell of relative calm. "A few minutes ago, the sound of several explosions was heard in the Karpan area of Sirik, in Hormozgan Province," the official IRNA news agency said. It added that "local sources have not yet disclosed the nature of these explosions." In late February, the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran, killing the country's supreme leader, along with senior military commanders. Iran has attempted to blockade the Strait of Hormuz, demanding all ships seek its authorization to cross. In peacetime, the strategic waterway carried around a fifth of the world's oil supplies. item.title: Early voting surges in states that could decide Senate control
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — Voter turnout is soaring compared with the last midterm election in many of the states that are expected to decide control of the U.S. Senate, according to an Associated Press analysis of early voting two weeks before Election Day. In Texas, early voting is up 74% compared with 2022. In Kansas it’s more than doubled. Maine, North Carolina and Ohio also have seen increases of more than 30% in early in-person and mail voting compared with the same point in 2022. Democrats are trying to flip Republican-held Senate seats in each of those states. In most of them, Republicans are accounting for a smaller share of advance voters than they did four years ago. The AP’s data, which runs through Tuesday, gives a snapshot of potential voter enthusiasm — and where it might be lacking — after early voting has opened in most states during a midterm cycle that has shifted in often unpredictable ways . Dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump’s tariffs, the persistently high cost of living , and high gas and diesel prices caused by the Iran war have generated political blowback against Republicans in places the party didn’t anticipate having to defend this year. Nationally, more than 13 million mail-in and early in-person votes have been cast, compared with 9 million at the same point in 2022. The increase also reflects a few additional states that expanded their early voting opportunities and ones that made more of their data available since the last midterms. Midterm elections typically favor the party out of power in Washington. With Republicans in control of both chambers of Congress and the White House, it's a distinctly different environment than 2022, when Democrats were in charge. Democrats energized by competitive Senate races in GOP-leaning states Senate Democrats were expected to face a tough map this cycle, defending a number of battlegrounds with only a few opportunities to flip seats in areas Trump won by single digits in 2024. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the chamber. But with gas and diesel prices up significantly from where they were a year ago and Trump increasingly unpopular among voters, Democrats have been wading into traditionally Republican states, hoping to win there for the first time in decades. Earlier this month, Republicans pulled back spending in a once-competitive North Carolina Senate race and dumped close to $12 million into Kansas, a state Trump won by 16 percentage points in 2024, to support GOP Sen. Roger Marshall against Democrat Adam Hamilton. Trump held a rally Monday in the state, where more than 55,000 people have cast their ballots so far — more than double the 27,000 people who had voted at this point in the cycle in 2022. That year, Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly narrowly won reelection while Republican Sen. Jerry Moran won overwhelmingly. Specific races seem to be drawing voters to the polls Texas also has seen a massive surge, even though early in-person voting just started Monday. The number of ballots cast two weeks from Election Day has reached nearly 1 million, up from roughly 550,000 at the same stage in 2022. Texas’ data doesn’t show ballots returned by party registration. The surge comes as Democrat James Talarico and Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton compete for the Senate seat currently held by GOP Sen. John Cornyn, whom Paxton defeated in a primary runoff with Trump’s endorsement. Democrats have targeted Paxton, who is benefiting from millions in outside spending, over corruption allegations and his impeachment by the Texas Legislature, though he was later acquitted. Talarico is trying to become the first Democrat to win statewide in more than three decades. Incumbent GOP Gov. Greg Abbott also is in an election fight against Democratic state lawmaker Gina Hinojosa. Ohio has top races up and down the ballot this year, with tight contests for U.S. Senate , House and governor. Total spending on the Ohio Senate race will reach close to $500 million, according to AdImpact. The increased attention is reflected in the votes, with 156,000 more ballots cast so far compared with 2022, a 30% increase. Some voting laws have changed in Ohio since 2022, including the state eliminating its grace period for receiving mail ballots, a change that forces voters to return those ballots earlier. In Maine, where five-term Republican Sen. Susan Collins is seeking reelection against Democrat Troy Jackson, there’s been an increase of 39% in ballots cast this year compared with two weeks before the election in the 2022 midterm. Advance vote hasn't increased in every competitive state In Michigan and Georgia, two states where Democrats are defending Senate seats, the total number of early votes cast is high, but similar to four years ago. Both states shattered their midterm voting records in 2022, with reproductive rights on the ballot in Michigan and a highly competitive U.S. Senate race in Georgia that year. Iowa, which voted three times for Trump in presidential years, has competitive contests for governor, Senate and in three of its four House districts. Early voting there two weeks out from the election is down about 6% from the same period four years ago. ___ Ryan Dubicki and Michaela Herbst of The Associated Press Election Services team contributed to this report from Washington. US Senate candidates Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, left, and Republican Mike Rogers shake hands after the debate on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, at WXYZ Channel 7 in Southfield, Michigan. - Robin Buckson/Pool/AP Michigan and Kansas held some of the final major Senate debates of the 2026 midterm elections on Wednesday night. And they were a study in contrasts. The Michigan Senate debate between Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers was bitterly personal and ferociously contested — as befits a contest that could decide the chamber’s majority. Each candidate had a simple task. El-Sayed, the former executive director of the Detroit Health Department, needed to pin Rogers, a former congressman, to the deeply unpopular President Donald Trump and his economy — and to assuage questions from moderates about his politics. Rogers is trying to win in a state currently run by Democrats while dragging Trump’s historically low approval ratings behind him. His only hope is to disqualify El-Sayed as an acceptable senator in the eyes of voters. The debate in Kansas was a little more genial, with less focus on Trump and plenty of focus on whether Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton would be too allied with the political left — from which he repeatedly sought to distance himself — to unseat GOP Sen. Roger Marshall. And Marshall, much more than Rogers, made a point of overtly appealing to Trump’s voters. Here are takeaways from the two crucial debates: Fierce debate over El-Sayed’s loyalty Rogers raised an extraordinary question: Is El-Sayed, a Muslim who was born in Michigan, really loyal to the United States? The charge came against a backdrop of searing false claims by Trump that the Democrat is a “jihadist.” Rogers claimed El-Sayed — who would be the first Muslim elected to the Senate — was bought off by the Muslim Brotherhood , an Islamist group founded in Egypt, and that he had donors who supported Iran-backed extremist organizations like Hamas and Hezbollah. “If you are going to go to the United States Senate, we need to know: Are you for America or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?” Rogers asked. “You can grin and you can smile and you can talk real pretty, but I’m going to tell you what: That is a risk to our national security.” El-Sayed, who has repudiated the Brotherhood, accused his opponent of a “shameful” attack. “To bring into question my commitment to the Constitution is really beneath you. I am proud of America. I’m proud to be an American. I’m proud of our Constitution that guarantees all of us the right to pray as we choose to pray,” he said. unknown content item - ‘Pattern of deception’ vs. ‘MAGA bingo’ Rogers also sought to play into the conceit that El-Sayed, as a progressive, is too far to the left of Michigan’s electorate, and he tried to reopen splits that were exposed between rival factions during the Democratic primary. He claimed that El-Sayed was “aligned” with the Democratic Socialists of America and wants “bigger government and more taxes.” El-Sayed describes himself as a capitalist and is not a member of the DSA, but he is supported by several members of the group, including New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who campaigned with him through Michigan’s Upper Peninsula last week. Rogers also tore at Democratic divides by appealing to disaffected supporters of El-Sayed’s defeated primary opponent. “You’re a Haley Stevens voter, and you came out of this, and you said, ‘Man, I just can’t do it. He’s too extreme’ … well, guess what, you have a home with us,” Rogers said in his closing statement. Ultimately, Rogers’ attacks on El-Sayed’s loyalties were aimed at advancing a broader argument — that the Democrat simply couldn’t be trusted — and one that implied, as Trump has, that he is not a fully authentic American. “There is, again, that whole pattern of deception,” Rogers said of El-Sayed’s claim to be in favor of strong border enforcement, using a refrain to which he frequently returned. Pushing back on El-Sayed’s denials that he wants to defund the police, Rogers claimed, “This guy has got new, false information about every 30 seconds.” El-Sayed countered multiple times that it was Rogers who was being untruthful and said he was playing a classic game of distraction practiced by Trump. He repeatedly said people should be playing “MAGA bingo” at home as they ticked off Rogers’ pre-planned buzzwords. But he warned: “When you are winning MAGA bingo, we are all losing.” The Trump factor Rogers, like every Republican candidate in the midterm elections, needs a way to separate himself from Trump’s most unpopular policies without alienating the president’s supporters, who must show up in vast numbers for him to win. He started with a complex pivot — admitting that the Michigan economy was in rough shape and that people were “hurting” but arguing that if Democrats got control of the Senate they’d make it even worse. This was a long way from Trump’s argument that Americans are living through an economic “golden age.” Rogers walked a fine line on tariffs, arguing that some were working to bring jobs home from Mexico and China, but that the trade war with Canada — a huge issue in Michigan’s border-state economy — was not well thought through. Rogers argued that Democratic control of Congress would cause higher taxes and higher costs, including for gasoline. El-Sayed had an easier task given huge public dissatisfaction with Trump’s handling of the economy; he claimed Rogers and the president stood “hip to hip.” He said that voters should send him to the Senate to ensure “money is going to be spent on you and your kids, rather than dropping bombs on somebody else and their kids.” He narrowed in on Rogers’ biggest vulnerability after the Republican said all his opponent did was say “Donald Trump” over and over again. El-Sayed countered by blaming the president’s decision to go to war with Iran for making the cost of living worse. “Yes, I am going to blame Donald Trump because this is Donald Trump’s economy. We are living in it,” El-Sayed said. “We are paying more for gas, more for groceries, defunding the Department of Education.” “We need to turn the page on Donald Trump, but that means we need to stand up to Donald Trump.” Kansas debate was more about Schumer than Trump Several states away, another Democratic Senate candidate was taking a very different approach. In red Kansas — a state Trump carried by 16 points — the name of the game for Hamilton was less about tying his opponent to Trump than assuring he’d be a candidate from the political middle. Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, right, and Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Adam Hamilton participate in a debate at WDAF TV in Kansas City, Missouri, on October 21. - Charlie Riedel/Pool/AP In fact, Democratic Senate Leader Chuck Schumer earned more mentions than Trump, as Marshall repeatedly sought to pitch Hamilton as enabling and supporting the New York Democrat’s agenda. When asked how he differed from the Democratic Party, Hamilton said former President Joe Biden’s border policies were a “disaster” and that he’s “not somebody who favors the Socialist Party.” He said he didn’t support Medicare for All or the Green New Deal, though he liked “parts” of the latter. “We’ve heard Chuck Schumer mentioned, I don’t know, 50 times? … Maybe 20 times so far,” Hamilton said. “I find that interesting. I’ve already said I wouldn’t support Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader if the Democrats [were] to control the Senate.” On the other side, Marshall distanced himself from Trump far less than Rogers has in Michigan. In fact, Marshall mostly bear-hugged Trump. When asked about Trump being unpopular even in Kansas, Marshall turned his response into an appeal to Trump supporters. “I’ve had multiple times when I’ve objected to the president before, but I do want to emphasize: We need the Trump voters to come out,” Marshall said. “And that would be my appeal tonight to people: If you want the Trump agenda to continue, if you want secure borders, if you want a strong military, if you want lower taxes … you need to come out, because we delivered on those things.” He also said later in the debate that Trump’s “tariffs are working.” When pressed again in his differences with Trump, he said he disagreed with ICE’s tactics in southwest Kansas — which many local Republicans recently objected to — and Trump’s plan to import beef. ICE was the big issue — and it got a little personal The ICE issue made for some of the most interesting portions of the debate, with Hamilton clearly seeking to turn it to his advantage. Marshall pitched the topic as an example of his ability to get Trump and his administration on the phone when he disagrees with something that’s happening. “The first thing I did when I saw what was going on in southwest Kansas (with ICE raids), I picked up the phone, called (Homeland Security) Secretary Markwayne Mullin and said, ‘Hey, I don’t think this is quite right. What’s going on?’” Marshall said. Marshall also signaled that there could be a broader conversation about immigration reform now that the border is more secure. He noted he has delivered many babies to undocumented parents. Hamilton pounced on that remark to cast the deportations that are currently taking place as heartless. “With all of those undocumented children that you delivered, did you also call ICE and ask them to be taken away?” Hamilton said. “What did you do with these people? You had compassion for them in delivering these children, but then you support quotas.” He said when he was in Hutchinson, Kansas, “There was a preschool teacher arrested in front of her children. That’s just not OK. We militarized and politicized ICE as opposed to them doing the important job they’re supposed to do, and that is protecting Americans from dangerous, dangerous people.” This story has been updated with additional details. item.title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion after jury finds company liable for deceiving users
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Diana Novak Jones Oct 21 (Reuters) - A judge in New Mexico ordered Meta Platforms on Wednesday to pay the state $25 billion after a jury found the company had misled consumers about the privacy of their data, hitting the company with one of the largest financial penalties in US history. The ruling came in a ‌case stemming from allegations that Cambridge Analytica, a British political consulting firm involved in Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign, obtained data from millions of Facebook users without their ‌consent. New Mexico had sued Meta, accusing it of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data. "Facebook's wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the ​heart of Facebook's core business practices," Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order, which came more than three weeks after the verdict. Mathew found that a penalty of more than $219 billion was warranted based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25 billion. In a statement, C.J. Mahoney, Meta's chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win on appeal. “This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new ‌rules for what people can say online." New Mexico Attorney General Raúl ⁠Torrez said in a statement after the ruling the penalty was one of the largest financial penalties against a corporation in US history. Meta previously faced a $5 billion penalty from the US Federal Trade Commission in 2019 over the Cambridge Analytica scandal. Six other states settled their lawsuits against Meta related ⁠to Cambridge Analytica for $459.2 million as part of a $17.1 billion multistate settlement the company reached in August to resolve states' claims that the company's platforms had harmed teen mental health. LAWSUIT FILED FIVE YEARS AGO New Mexico's attorney general sued Meta in 2021 following revelations that Cambridge Analytica had harvested personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app. The state accused Meta of lying to Facebook users ​in ​New Mexico about who had access to their data and its handling of hate speech and misinformation posted ​on the platform. It alleged the company knew third parties had broad ‌access to users' data and tolerated hate speech or other harmful content when it benefited the company's bottom line. Cambridge Analytica, now defunct, used the data for voter profiling and targeting. "It has been a long time coming holding Big Tech accountable," Torrez told a press conference in Albuquerque after Wednesday's ruling. "I think today's judgment is a clear break with that past and a very clear warning to those in this space and beyond that we intend to protect our people and protect our consumers." Mathew's decision comes as Meta faces thousands of lawsuits and pressure from lawmakers over the impact of Instagram and Facebook on teen mental health, with another trial slated to begin next week. Earlier this year, New Mexico won $942 million in a pair of trials against Meta over ‌claims it facilitated sexual exploitation of young people on Instagram and Facebook and misled consumers about the ​platforms' safety. Analyst Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson & Co, called the latest New Mexico ruling costly ​but unlikely to impact the company's value. "Meta is worth nearly two trillion dollars, and ​will likely continue to appeal these cases and drag them out," Luria said. EXPERTS EXPECT LONG APPEAL FIGHT Jurors in September had found that the company and ‌its leadership made 26 misleading statements on data privacy, hate speech and ​other subjects. Multiplying those statements by their potential ​audience, they said the company had committed more than 43 million violations of New Mexico’s consumer protection laws. At a hearing on October 1, Randi McGinn, a lawyer for New Mexico, had asked Mathew to award the state between $35 billion and $40 billion. "This court should speak to Meta in the only language it understands, which is money, and the ​value of its stock price," McGinn said. In court filings, Meta urged ‌Mathew to cap the penalties at $3.45 billion. The evidence showed that Meta does not sell user data and New Mexico did not prove that any consumer had ​actually been misled, the company said in court filings. (Reporting by Diana Novak Jones in Chicago, additional reporting by Andrew Hay in New Mexico and Jaspreet Singh ​and Anzar Mehraj in Bangalore. Editing by Alexia Garamfalvi, Nia Williams, Aurora Ellis and Stephen Coates) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://finance.yahoo.com/news/meta-ordered-pay-25-billion-172737485.html

item.title: Rep. Ilhan Omar says death threats are forcing her to move after federal raid
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) said she will have to move out of her apartment in Washington, D.C., because of threats she’s received after federal agents executed a search warrant at her residence last week as part of an immigration fraud probe . “Obviously, I can’t continue to live there … Because our address has been public and with the death threats that I deal with, it’s no longer going to be feasible to be in that house and have my kids visiting off and on, having people track them,” she told MS NOW’s Chris Hayes in a Wednesday interview. The congresswoman, who also has a residence in her home state of Minnesota, told Hayes she woke up at 6 a.m. on Oct. 12 to learn federal agents had “surrounded her house" in D.C. She said the agents provided her a search warrant before going “room by room” and seizing 17 items, including her phone and other electronics. President Trump and his administration have claimed that Omar’s father lied about her age when she obtained U.S. citizenship in 2000 after their family emigrated from Somalia. The Democratic lawmaker has denied these allegations and accused the Trump administration of waging a “campaign of political intimidation” against her in a social media post following the raid. “If you had so confidently said I’ve committed a crime, why are you not saying in the beginning … we’re going to subpoena people, we’re going to do a grand jury, we’re going to try to find evidence that would lead to an indictment? It’s just it’s all bizarre,” Omar said in the Wednesday interview. Last week, The Washington Post reported that federal officials under the first Trump administration reviewed Omar’s immigration records in 2019 but did not find evidence of fraud. The president has for years attacked Omar in social media posts and speeches for her political views and background. During comments to reporters in the Oval Office on Wednesday, Trump slammed Omar as a “sick, very dishonest person … who hates our country.” “I hope they treat her fairly, but she’s a very dishonest person,” he added. The Minnesota progressive said she has received an outpouring of support from her Democratic colleagues. She also responded to former President Obama’s statement condemning the Trump administration’s investigation into her as “appalling.” “I think a lot of the conspiracy world that I find myself in is the conspiracy world that was created around him, and so while some people might feel reserved in some of the information that they hear from these people, I think he is acutely capable of seeing what this is,” she said. Omar told MS NOW on Wednesday she feels “confident” that she has done nothing wrong. “I am a person of enormous faith,” she said. “And I know that … if I continue to live my truth, if I continue to fight for the right things, if I continue to stand up to bullies and people who are carrying out ungodly corruption, I’m going to be OK.” Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. item.title: Oregon teacher says she played dead after being shot in elementary school attack
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Wednesday was the first day since the shooting that students in the greater Bend-La Pine Schools district in Oregon returned to classes, although not at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, where the shooting occurred. (Payton Bruni / AFP via Getty) A teacher who was shot by a teenage gunman in a Bend, Oregon, elementary school last week said she saw the attacker and tried to shut the classroom door, “but the shooter was already there.” Becky Drury said she was shot at close range in the rampage at Silver Rail Elementary School on Thursday. “Lying on the floor, I saw that my left hand was almost completely severed from the gunshot, and my other arm was also severely injured,” Drury said in a statement Wednesday. “I could not get up, defend myself, or protect anyone else,” she said. “So, I did the only thing I could do, which was to pretend to be dead in the hope he would not shoot me again.” Three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and a 25-year-old teacher were killed in the attack, which began around 1 p.m., officials said. The gunman was fatally shot by a bystander who saw him fire at a truck and enter the school, police have said. The bystander followed the 16-year-old gunman and shot him as another teacher was wrestling with him over the weapon, according to police. The motive remained under investigation Wednesday. Investigators are looking into whether the shooter viewed any extremist material online, including material associated with “nihilistic violent extremism,” also known as NVE, two senior law enforcement officials briefed on the investigation told NBC News. The gun was purchased legally, Bend police said in a statement Wednesday. Police have said that it was a Maverick 88 pump-action 12-gauge shotgun and that the shooter used birdshot, buckshot and slugs. Police have not said who purchased the gun. Two senior law enforcement officials previously told NBC News that the shooter’s mother bought it in August, around the time of his birthday. “Bend Police detectives continue this complex investigation. They have served search warrants at the shooting suspect’s home, as well as on his electronic devices and his social media accounts on a variety of platforms,” police said in a statement Wednesday. “That work continues, and it takes time,” the police department said. Three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and teacher Megan Lambert, 25, were killed in the Oct. 13 attack. (Mathieu Lewis-Rolland / Getty) Students in the greater Bend-La Pine Schools district returned to class Wednesday, although not at Silver Rail Elementary, where the shooting occurred. “Through heartfelt artwork and messages of love, they are making sure every student who walks through the doors knows they are cared for, supported and loved,” the district said Tuesday as it prepared to welcome most students back. Authorities have publicly identified two of the victims who were killed, 5-year-old Rhoam Summer and teacher Megan Lambert. Drury, the wounded teacher, said in her statement that she heard a noise last week and went to investigate. “Here is what I remember: Once I realized something was happening outside, I ran to see what was going on,” she said. “I then saw the shooter and immediately ran back into the classroom. I turned to shut the door behind me, but the shooter was already there,” she said. Drury said that there was nothing more she could have done and that “I was shot before I had any chance to act.” “What happened in that classroom was unimaginable, and like so many in this community, my heart is broken for everyone affected by this tragedy,” she said. “My thoughts are with those who were hurt, those we lost, their families, our school, and the Bend community,” she said. “I am truly grateful for the kindness and support we have received as we face the difficult days ahead together.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/teacher-survived-bend-shooting-tried-close-door-shooter-was-already-rcna604904

item.title: Trump admin. seeks emergency Supreme Court order to restart Texas border wall
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Andrew Chung Oct 21 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump's administration asked the US Supreme Court on Wednesday to let it proceed with a plan to build a US-Mexico border ‌barrier in a remote region in West Texas that includes Big Bend National Park. The ‌Justice Department filed an emergency request for the court to lift a federal judge's order halting wall construction in the region ​while a lawsuit against the project brought by an environmental group and other challengers plays out. The Republican president has long touted building or reinforcing barriers along the US-Mexico border as a signature part of his anti-immigration policies. But his administration's push to extend border infrastructure into the national park, around 250 miles (400 ‌km) southeast of El Paso, has ⁠faced opposition from local officials, conservationists and some Texas Republicans. The lawsuit was brought by the Center for Biological Diversity, a Big Bend-area river guide and a ⁠group seeking to preserve a historic church in Ruidosa, Texas, that says its fragile adobe structure is threatened by the border construction. The plaintiffs challenged a series of waivers issued by the US Department of Homeland ​Security to ​expedite construction of roads and barriers in the Big ​Bend region, avoiding the application of ‌a variety of environmental and conservation laws. Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and the current Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who issued the waivers between February and July, found the region to be an "area of high illegal entry," requiring additional barriers to control the border. US District Judge Kathleen Cardone in El Paso issued an injunction on October 2 halting the construction. In an opinion issued later, the judge found ‌that the waivers exceeded the authority of Noem and ​Mullin. The Justice Department in its request urged the Supreme Court ​to pause or overturn Cardone's injunction. "Even assuming ​that the secretary's waiver authority implicates a question of 'vast economic and political significance,' ‌Congress did clearly authorize the secretary both ​to build border barriers and ​to waive legal requirements in order to facilitate their expeditious construction," the Justice Department wrote. In August, the administration paused construction in Big Bend after the project drew bipartisan criticism over ​its potential impact on the ‌park's landscape and wildlife. Crews had begun clearing land in the park for roads and ​border security infrastructure, prompting protests and lawsuits seeking to halt the work. (Reporting by Andrew ​Chung in New York; Editing by Will Dunham) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/trump-asks-us-supreme-court-220351669.html

item.title: Social Security corrects millions of records. Could your benefits be affected?
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The U.S. Social Security Administration (SSA) said Tuesday that it has corrected millions of records associated with nearly 15% of active Social Security numbers (SSN), which it said was part of an effort to prevent fraud. The agency called it the "most comprehensive SSN record clean-up" in its 91-year history, and said it had added 17 million missing dates of death to its records and updated citizenship information for about 25 million records. It is also working to correct another 8.5 million records with inaccurate citizenship status and has introduced stronger internal controls to prevent future data-entry errors. "This is the first time SSA has undertaken an effort of this scale, and I am proud of the work we have done to strengthen the foundation of identity data relied upon throughout government and the economy," Commissioner Frank J. Bisignano said in a statement outlining the work the agency had carried out. The SSA said the changes are intended to improve the accuracy of records used by federal and state agencies to verify identities, prevent fraud and ensure government benefits are paid correctly. Here's what we know about the cleanup so far — and what it could mean for your account. What exactly has Social Security changed? The SSA cleanup focuses on the Social Security number (SSN) database, which government agencies use to verify identities and help administer benefits. According to the SSA , millions of records were missing a date of death or citizenship information. To address those gaps, the agency used information from its own systems and the State Department to add missing dates of death. It also used data from the Department of Homeland Security to update citizenship records. The SSA said the corrections are intended to improve the accuracy of its records, prevent fraud and reduce improper payments across government programs. The agency has also introduced stronger internal controls designed to prevent future errors caused by manual data entry. Could the cleanup affect your benefits or records? Accurate death and citizenship records help determine who is eligible for Social Security benefits and prevent incorrect payments. Death records are particularly important for survivor benefits, which provide financial support to eligible family members after someone receiving or eligible for Social Security dies. However, the SSA has not said whether its latest corrections have changed anyone's benefit payments or eligibility, or whether anyone has had problems with their records. The accuracy of death records has drawn scrutiny before. Earlier this year, a former senior SSA official alleged in a whistleblower disclosure that Homeland Security officials, with involvement from Department of Government Efficiency staff, pushed the agency to mark as many as 2.7 million people as dead without sufficient evidence. The former official said the plan was rejected but alleged that more than 6,000 people were incorrectly recorded as dead in a separate April 2025 update. The SSA has denied adding the proposed 2.7 million names to its Death Master File. Do you need to check your Social Security information? The SSA has not announced any new requirements for people to check or update their Social Security information after the cleanup. However, people can review some of their information through their online my Social Security account , including their earnings history and, for those receiving benefits, payment details. Anyone who notices an error in their records or experiences an unexpected interruption to their benefits can contact Social Security directly to ask about the issue and how to resolve it. The agency has not said that the latest cleanup requires beneficiaries to submit new documents or take any other action.
